..(Thursday night through Tuesday)
Issued at 541 AM EDT WED OCT 14 2026

The long term forecast period is defined by a significant change in 
sensible weather conditions across eastern Kentucky. While the 
period begins Thursday night with unusually mild conditions 
overnight, a potent cold front should sweep through the area early 
Friday and usher in a noticeably cooler and drier airmass for the 
weekend. In fact, Saturday's forecast features the coldest 
temperatures of the season thus far. A widespread frost is looking 
increasingly likely on Saturday night, but temperatures are forecast 
to moderate back towards climatological norms under fair skies early 
next week. 

The period begins with a sharp trough ejecting southeast out of 
Canada, phasing with a leeward Rocky Mountain trough to yield a 
deeper, positively-tilted feature over the Upper Midwest on Thursday 
evening. Vertically-stacked southwesterly flow around the base of 
that trough will advect warm air into the atmospheric column over 
the Ohio River Valley. The aforementioned boundary is accordingly 
forecast to lift back north as a warm front on Thursday night, and a 
deepening surface low should emerge over the Great Lakes by Friday 
morning. In response to the tightening pressure gradient, winds will 
become breezy overnight. This will prevent the area's conventional 
ridge-valley splits from materializing in this time frame, as the 
boundary layer should remain well mixed. Given the lack of 
decoupling and the warm air advection regime in place, Thursday 
night's temperature forecast looks unseasonably mild. Expect a muted 
diurnal heating curve, with lows in the mid to upper 60s. 

Friday's high temperatures will be pretty similar to Thursday 
night's lows, as the cold front associated with this system will be 
on the doorstep of the JKL CWA on Friday morning. (In fact, latest 
modeling suggests that in some locations Friday's high temperatures 
will occur at or shortly after midnight.) There should be enough 
forced lift for some generic rain showers over the CWA during and 
after Friday's frontal passage, but the greatest impacts from this 
boundary will stem from its cold air advection. The sharp nature of 
the parent troughing aloft and the fairly tight surface pressure 
gradient in this set up collectively suggest that there will be a 
pronounced shift from breezy southwesterly winds to gustier 
northwesterly winds as frontal passage occurs on Friday. 
Northwesterly wind gusts in the 20-30 mph range are likely on Friday 
afternoon/evening before the pressure gradient weakens overnight. 
The winds will retain their northwesterly orientation through 
Saturday morning, which will help them usher a noticeably cooler and 
drier airmass into the region for the weekend. That efficient cold 
air advection may actually cause temperatures to decrease during the 
afternoon hours on Friday, with widespread temps in the 50s by 
Friday evening and the upper 30s to 40s on Saturday morning.

Northerly winds associated with a post-frontal surface high will 
keep the cold air advection going on Saturday. High temps will 
struggle to make it out of the 50s, and afternoon dewpoints should 
plummet towards the low/mid 30s area-wide. Under mostly clear skies 
and slackening winds, Saturday night looks to be the coldest night 
of the season thus far. Efficient radiational cooling and those dry 
dewpoint values favor widespread low temperatures in the 30s and 
frost potential in more than just the typical cold spots. Near-
freezing temperatures cannot be ruled out in the most sheltered and 
shadiest valley locales, but a widespread freeze appears unlikely. 
Nevertheless, frost/freeze headline products will need to be 
considered as this time frame approaches and forecast confidence 
continues to improve. Agricultural interests and recreational 
gardeners are accordingly encouraged to review any relevant frost 
preparedness plans and stay tuned for potential product issuance. 

The progressive nature of the overarching synoptic weather pattern 
prevents this chillier air from becoming permanent. It is not winter 
yet, and winter precipitation is not expected. The postfrontal high 
should shift east on Sunday as the previous trough axis aloft swings 
through New England. Modeled height rises amidst a building ridge 
suggest that temperatures will moderate under fair skies in the 
latter stages of the forecast period. Expect highs to rebound into 
the 60s on Sunday and then towards the 70 degree mark early next 
week. Dewpoints will be slow to recover to the pre-frontal values 
forecast at the beginning of the period, but the approach of a 
southern-stream shortwave trough on Monday should return some 
moisture to the column by Monday night into Tuesday. So, while an 
additional round of patchy frost is possible in the coldest valleys 
on Sunday night, Eastern Kentucky's typical autumnal river valley 
fog should return to the forecast on Monday night.
